text:
Count the number of picks per analyst
My first step in analyzing data is to characterize it by generating basic summary statistics. Looking at the first (2) rows of my table which include a header row as well as a single row of data, I can see that some rows have information represented as categories and some as numbers. This is a valuable distinction because I will need different methods to summarize numerical and categorical data. Numbers are easy to summarize because I can use standard mathematical algorithms like summing and counting. In the case of categorical data, the mathematical relationships between categories are not obvious. However, one thing that I can do is to count the number of occurrences of each category.

How do I know which columns contain what kind of data?
In order to design a robust system of analysis, I want to make my analytical framework as generalizeable as possible. This means minimalizing the amount of assumptions I make about my data. To understand the type of data present in each of my columns I can use a list comprehension with the isinstance() function in order to get a list of the data type (string, integer, float, etc.) of each item in that column which I have represented in Python using a list. I can then convert that list of types into a set, which is a special type of list, so that I only retain unique values of the original list. This set will include all of the types of data present in my column. And because each type will only be present once in the set, I can count the length of the set to find out how many data types are present. If all of the data types are numerical, then I can apply mathematical algorithms to understand that column. If the column contains numerical and categorical data then I can treat that data as categorical since I do not have a method to naively predict how to map categorial data to numerical values.


A note on list comprehensions
List comprehensions follow the general syntax of “do this for each of these in those”. For example, calculate the length of this string for each string in those strings where a string is a string of characters.

title: Player database: basic looping structure
text:
In the last post I was prototyping a method for storing player data as metadata in a database. My approach was to store all of the words in an index.json file. This would be the central data file which all of the othe metadata files would reference.
One of the challenges I encountered was how to structure my data to enable the looping mechanism that I envisioned to validate search results. If I structured the index.json file as a dictionary then it would be easy for me to look up the query word in the index and find all of the places it occurred in the database.
The database will be English language queryable which means that I initially need to look up the words in the index and then find the places they occur in the metadata files and then use graph traversal to find the most efficient route that connects all of the query words.
The thing I was struggling with is that once I have the route through the metadata I need to then remap the metadata values back to the data values stored in the central index.json file. The metadata files reference indices - that is how the database is structured; related data fields are all stored at the same index.
The conclusion I came to was that it would be easiest to store the index as a list for reverse lookup and as a dictionary for lookup.
I need to do reverse lookup because values in my metadata files can be composites of words in the index.json file.
And then I decided that I was trying to do too much too fast and I need to focus on smaller steps.

def file_traversal_search(current_file_path, files_to_look_for, files_traversed=[]):
    """Find a path from the current file to one of the ones I am looking for.

    Args:
        current_file_path (str): The path of the current file.
        files_to_look_for (list): A list of eligible destination files.
        files_traversed (list): A list of the files that have already been traversed during search.

    Returns:
        files_traversed (list): Once a destination file has been found this function will return the list of files traversed.
    """ 

    # Add the current file to the list of files traversed
    files_traversed.append(current_file_path)
    print(current_file_path, files_to_look_for)    

    # Check if the current file is the one the function is looking for. If so, then
    # the function has completed its job and will return the list of files
    # that it traversed to find the file or files it was looking for.
    if current_file_path in files_to_look_for:
        return files_traversed

    with open(current_file_path, 'r') as file_handle:
        file_data = json.load(file_handle)
    # The path to the next file in the database is always stored as the last element.
    next_file_path = file_data[-1]
 
    if next_file_path in files_to_look_for:
        files_traversed.append(next_file_path)
        return files_traversed
    else:
        return file_traversal_search(next_file_path, files_to_look_for, files_traversed)

text:
Find all of the looping paths between query words
I can find all of the paths between each word using the looping_file_search() function that I previously defined.

# This list is not actually sorted yet
sorted_word_location_lists = query_word_location_lists

# Add the first node to the end of the list to complete the loop
sorted_word_location_lists.append(sorted_word_location_lists[0])

edges = []
for query_word_index, this_word_locations in enumerate(sorted_word_location_lists):
    #print(query_word_index, this_word_locations)
    
    # Break the loop once I reach the end of the list of words
    if query_word_index >= len(sorted_word_location_lists) - 1:
        break
    locations_to_look_for = sorted_word_location_lists[query_word_index + 1]
    files_to_look_for = [location["source"] for location in locations_to_look_for]
    for this_location in this_word_locations:
        traversal_paths = []         

        # Find a path to the next location
        path = file_traversal_search(this_location["source"], files_to_look_for, files_traversed=[])
        next_source = path[-1]
        #print(f"Path from {this_location["source"]} to {next_source}: {path}.")

        # Now that I have found a looping path between two adjacent
        # words in my query I want to calculate the minimum index
        # distance between those words in those source locations.
        this_source_locations = [location for location in this_word_locations if location["source"] == this_location["source"]]
        next_source_locations = [location for location in locations_to_look_for if location["source"] == next_source]

        this_location_indexes = set(location["index"] for location in this_source_locations)
        next_location_indexes = list(set(location["index"] for location in next_source_locations))

        if 0 in next_location_indexes:
            # Add every index of this word  as an index of the next
            # word if it is a variable.
            next_location_indexes.extend(this_location_indexes)
            next_location_indexes.remove(0)
        #print(f"next_location_indexes: {next_location_indexes}")   
 
        # First I need to find all of the locations that match
        # this source from my 
        index_pairs = list(itertools.product(this_location_indexes, next_location_indexes))
        #print(index_pairs)
        index_products = [{"start": index_pair[0], "end": index_pair[1], "score": index_pair[0] * index_pair[1]} for index_pair in index_pairs]
        
        index_products = sorted(index_products, key=lambda index_product: index_product["score"])

        # I have deprecated this logic in favor of the above where I use a
        # list comprehension to remove any products with zero scores.
        optimal_index = index_products[0]
        if optimal_index["score"] == 0:
            optimal_index["score"] = 1
            # I need to change the variable index to an index of an actual
            # value. I do not know which word has an index of zero so I
            # will change both start and end indexes to the maximum.
            optimal_index["start"] = max([optimal_index["start"], optimal_index["end"]])
            optimal_index["end"] = max([optimal_index["start"], optimal_index["end"]])

        # Once I have found one of the files to look for I 
        # need to then find the minimum index distance from the
        # current source to the source that I was looking for.
        path_dictionary = {
                           "start": {"source": path[0], "index": optimal_index["start"]},
                           "end": {"source": path[-1], "index": optimal_index["end"]},
                           "path": path,
                           "steps": len(path),
                           "index_score": optimal_index["score"]
        }
        traversal_paths.append(path_dictionary)
    edges.append(traversal_paths)

Now that I have refined the in memory structure of my database I want to revisit my search algorithm and refactor it so that it is more understandable. I previously designed it to interact with database metadata serialized as JSON files. These slow read operations were baked in to my core algorithm which also made it slow and locked me an into an in drive structure.
I am still somewhat confused as to how my search algorithm works because I was trying a bunch of things when I implemented it. I want to pare it back to the bare minimum viability so that I can understand it and then start layering features on top of it.




Now that I am thinking about search I realize that having all of my columns in the same dictionary would probably make it easier to do column traversal. On second thought, maybe not. The index peforms a special role and for the sake of traversal search I do not ever need to visit the index because the index is for mapping metadata to data and search traversal is simply pattern recognition which can be accomplished with metadata as well as with data.

def add_new_word_to_index(word, column_name, position, index_list, word_positions):

def transpose_matrix(matrix):
    """Transpose a matrix represented as a list of lists.

    Arguments:
        matrix (list): A list of equal length lists.
    
    Returns:
        (list): A list of lists where all of the values have been transposed.
    """

    transposed_matrix = [[row[index] for row in row_matrix] for index in range(len(row_matrix[0]))]
    return transposed_matrix

def find_query_loops_too(metadata_column_dictionary, query_word_locations_list):
    """
    Arguments:
        metadata_column_dictionary (dict): A dictionary of the database represented as references to the index.
        query_word_locations_lists (list): A list of lists of locations where each word in the query can be found. Each inner list corresponds to the word in the query at the same position.
    """
    print(f"Query word locations list: {query_word_locations_list}.")
    query_word_locations_list.append(query_word_locations_list[0])

    edges_list = []
    for query_word_position, query_word_locations in enumerate(query_word_locations_list):
        if query_word_position >= len(query_word_locations_list) - 1:
            break
        
        for current_location in query_word_locations:
            print(f"Current location: {current_location}.")

            current_column = current_location["column"]
            # Use this list to filter locations of the next query word
            columns_in_loop = get_columns_in_loop(
                                                  metadata_column_dictionary,
                                                  current_column,
                                                  columns_traversed=[])
            current_positions = current_location["positions"]

            # Create a list of locations that can be found on this loop.
            # Location format: {"column": (1), "positions": [1]}
            next_locations = query_word_locations_list[query_word_position + 1]
            next_viable_locations = [
                                     location for location
                                     in next_locations
                                     if location["column"] in columns_in_loop]
            print(f"Next viable locations: {next_viable_locations}.")
            
            # What if a location points to the column name? The positions are effectively wildcards.
            # reference: https://stackoverflow.com/a/58265773
            [location.update(positions=current_positions) for location in next_viable_locations if location['positions']==[0]]
            print(f"Next wildcard locations: {next_viable_locations}.")

            
            # Maybe I should expand my locations. Currently I support multiple positions
            # per column. I can create separate items for all of those.
            start_pointers = [
                              (current_location["column"], position)
                              for position in current_location["positions"]
            ]
            print(f"Start pointers: {start_pointers}.")

            end_pointers = []
            for location in next_viable_locations:
                for position in location['positions']:
                    end_pointers.append((location["column"], position))
            print(f"End pointers: {end_pointers}.")

            endpoint_pairs = list(itertools.product(start_pointers, end_pointers))
            print(f"Endpoint pairs: {endpoint_pairs}.")

            endpoint_scores = [
                               calculate_positions_score(endpoints[0][1], endpoints[1][1])
                               for endpoints in endpoint_pairs]
            print(f"Endpoint scores: {endpoint_scores}.")
            max_endpoints_score = max(endpoint_scores)            

            scored_endpoints = zip(endpoint_pairs, endpoint_scores)
            max_score_endpoints = [
                                   endpoints for endpoints
                                   in scored_endpoints
                                   if endpoints[1] == max_endpoints_score]
            print(f"Max score endpoints: {max_score_endpoints}.")

            # Generate a list of viable edges
            max_score_edges = []
            for endpoints in max_score_endpoints:
                metadata_values = endpoints[0]
                score = endpoints[1]        
        
                start_reference = metadata_values[0]
                end_reference = metadata_values[1]
                
                edge_dictionary = {
                                   "start": start_reference,
                                   "end": end_reference,
                                   "score": score
                }
                max_score_edges.append(edge_dictionary)
            edges_list.append(max_score_edges)
    return edges_list

def find_query_loops(list_of_location_dictionaries, metadata_column_dictionary):
    """
    
    Arguments:
        list_of_location_dictionaries (list): Column names represented as tuples of the primary indexes of each word in the name of the column.
        metadata_column_dictionary (dict): A dictionary containing all of the database connections where keys are metadata-translated column keys and values are metadata-translated columns.
    """
    # Add the first node to the end of the list to complete the loop
    list_of_location_dictionaries.append(list_of_location_dictionaries[0])

    edges = []
    #edges = {}
    for query_word_position, this_word_locations in enumerate(list_of_location_dictionaries):
        # Break the loop once I reach the end of the list of words
        if query_word_position >= len(list_of_location_dictionaries) - 1:
            break
        
        # The locations lists are dictionaries with the column name and position
        locations_to_look_for = list_of_location_dictionaries[query_word_position + 1]
        columns_to_look_for = locations_to_look_for.keys()    
    
        traversal_paths = []
        for this_column in this_word_locations.keys():
            #traversal_paths = []

            # Find a path to the next location
            viable_paths = column_traversal_search(
                                                   metadata_column_dictionary,
                                                   this_column,

            )
            print(f"Viable paths from column {this_column} to columns {columns_to_look_for}: {viable_paths}.")
            traversal_paths.append(viable_paths)
            for viable_path in viable_paths.values():
                path_dictionary = {
                                   "start": viable_path[0],
                                   "end": viable_path[-1],
                                   "columns_traversed": viable_path,
                                   "number_of_steps": len(viable_path)
                }
                edges.append(path_dictionary)

    return edges

def calculate_edge_score(edge, edge_position, column_position_dictionaries):
    start_position = column_position_dictionaries[edge_position][tuple(edge['start'])]
    end_position = column_position_dictionaries[edge_position + 1][tuple(edge['end'])]

    if start_position == 0 or end_position == 0:
        max_position = max([start_position, end_position])
        start_position = max_position
        end_position = max_position

    position_score = abs(start_position - end_position)
    edge_score = position_score * edge["number_of_steps"]
    return edge_score


def choose_loop(list_of_viable_edges, previous_node=None):
    chosen_edges = []
    for position, viable_edges in enumerate(list_of_viable_edges):
        if previous_node:
            matching_viable_edges = [edge for edge in viable_edges if edge['start'] == previous_node]
        else:
            matching_viable_edges = viable_edges
        
        sorted_viable_edges = sorted(matching_viable_edges, key=lambda edge: edge['score'])
        chosen_edge = sorted_viable_edges[0]
        chosen_edges.append(chosen_edge)
    return chosen_edges


def get_response_documents(edges):
    response_node_references = []
    for edge_path in edges:
        start_node = edge_path["start"]
        response_node_references.append(start_node)
    return response_node_references

text:
In my previous post I focussed on refining the structure of my database in order to enable importing data. I decided to disentangle the storage method from the data structure by removing file references from the data. This will provide me more flexibility in structuring and storing my data.
Now that I have made some changes to structure I want to revisit my search algorithm and get it to work again while also whittling away some of the extraneous operations that I initially added. By simplifying it to the most fundamental methods I can better understand how it works.
When I import a table into a Circuity database each column in the table is stored individually in the metadata_dictionary. Each key is the name of a column and the value contains all of the values for that column. Items in the column that contain strings are converted to metadata referenes and numerical values are left as is.
The metadata dictionary allows me to store all the information of the database natively in Python data structures so that there are not any file reading intrinsic to the database operations. I will need to refactor my search mechanism to fit this new model.




Answer: Yes.
Each column in my database includes the column name at position zero. Now that I have a metadata dictionary that maps the name of the column to the values, do I still want to maintain this structure?
One of the concepts I want to incorporate into the database is that of being able to represent all of the connections between data as metadata so that I can share knowledge without sharing data. By storing all of the information necessary to perform search operations within the column values I can share new data structures that allow fully reproducible search operations without having to share the data itself. And for the sake of sharing these patterns I will have to serialize the metadata to files.



Answer: Yes.
When I import data from a comma separated values file I consider the structure of that file to represnt a loop because every column in the table is related to every other column. In the case where I import (2) files into my database that both include the column age I want some way to distinguish which column is most relevant to my query and the way I can do that is by looking at the other columns in the loop.
If I have (5) people named “Jarrian Jackson” in my database and I search “Jarrian Jackson age” I can imagine getting back (5) results. If I search “Jarrian Jackson team age” I can imagine only getting results for any Jarrian Jackson that plays on a team if both team and age are part of the same loop. In this way the loop provides important context for determining result validity.



Answer: Yes.
I thought about moving this information to a separate file that only defines the columns in the loop. A problem I have with that is that now I need to read (2) data structures to figure out where to go next and then I need to worry about maintaining the relationship between those structures and that abstraction makes the connection more tenuous and fragile when I want to make my internal database structure as robust as possible. For that reason I include the name and the name of the next partner of that column in the column itself.



Answer: Yes.
I want to use loops to organize my database and facilitate search. I want all of the information necessary to traverse these loops to be stored within each column. Because the loop name and the column name are essential for identifying the appropriate next step in a search I want both of these pieces of information together in each column.

Changing references to locations

I am using the term reference to indicate a dictionary that points to a column and a position. In that sense using references in the index is not so helpful because it is abstract even if it is accurate.
index_list = [{'word': 'index', 'references': [{'source': 'index', 'index': 0}]}]
If I change references to locations it becomes clearer to me that this index is pointing out all of the locations where I can find this word.
index_list = [{'word': 'index', 'locations': [{'source': 'index', 'index': 0}]}]

Changing source to column

When I chose the name source I was thinking about data storage rather than data structure. Now that I am abstracting away the storage component I can focus on words which describe how my data is organized. And column indicates that I am organizing my database into columns and indicates a relationship to columnar databases. This also makes clear that the index is itself a column.
index_list = [{'word': 'index', 'locations': [{'column': 'index', 'index': 0}]}]

Changing index to position

I have been using the term “index” so much that I confuse myself when trying to figure out what I mean. By changing the reference key from index to position I can disentangle the index column from the position that I am referencing within a particular column.
index_list = [{'word': 'index', 'locations': [{'column': 'index', 'position': 0}]}]
Now when I look at this entry in the index I can more inuitively understand what it means because the terms are more specific.



Answer: No.
The index is a special column which contains the mapping from data to metadata. In that way it is structured differently from every other column in the database. It also contains the private keys that unlock the meaning of the rest of the database. I also use it differently from every other column.

def initialize_database():
    """Generate the index and associated data structures that are at the core of the database.
    
    Returns:
        (list): The primary index of words in the database stored as dictionaries with references to each location of each word in the database.
        (dict): The primary index represented as a dictionary where the key is the word and the value is a list of locations where that word occurs in the metadata dictionary.
        (dict): A mapping of each word to its position in the primary index.

def transpose_matrix(matrix):

def import_comma_separated_values(csv_file, index_list, index_dictionary, word_indexes):
    """Import values from a comma separated values file into the database.

    Arguments:
        csv_file (str): The path to a comma separated values file.
        index_list (list): The primary database index.
        index_dictionary (dict): Mapping of each word to its database locations.
        word_indexes (dict): Mapping of each word to its position in the primary index.

    Returns:
        index_list: Updated with new word locations.
        word_references: Updated with new words.
        word_indexes: Updated with new indexes.
    """
    loop_name = csv_file.split('/')[-1].split('.')[0]
    
    # Read file into a matrix of rows
    row_matrix = []
    with open(csv_file) as csv_handle:
        csv_reader = csv.reader(csv_handle)
        for row in csv_reader:
            row_matrix.append(row)
    
    # Convert the matrix of rows to columns
    column_matrix = [[row[index] for row in row_matrix] for index in range(len(row_matrix[0]))]

    # Convert the actual column values to references to the primary index
    metadata_columns = []
    for column in column_matrix:
        metadata_column = []

    # Write metadata columns to files

        os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(file_path), exist_ok=True)
        with open(file_path, 'w') as file_handle:
            json.dump(column, file_handle)
    return metadata_columns



def convert_reference_to_string(reference, index_list):
    #print(f"Converting reference '{reference}' to string.")
    if not isinstance(reference, dict):
        # Numbers stored in metadata files can be returned as is.
        return reference
    
    indexes = reference["indexes"]
    #word_dicts = [index_list[index] for index in indexes]


    words = [convert_index_to_word(index, index_list) for index in indexes]
    
    #words = [word_dict["word"] for word_dict in word_dicts]
    this_string = (" ").join(words)
    #print(f"Converted reference {reference} to string {this_string}.")
    return this_string


def convert_index_to_word(index, index_list):
    #print(f"Converting index ({index}) to word.")
    # The word_dict contains the value of the word as other metadata.
    word_dict = index_list[index]
    word = word_dict["word"]
    #print(f"Converted index ({index}) to word {word}.")
    return word


def convert_string_to_reference(string, column_name, row_index, index_list, word_references, word_indexes):
    #print(f"Converting string '{string}' to reference.")
    # All values can be stored as strings. In order to determine whether
    # a value contains words or numbers I am going to try converting it
    # to a float which is a numeric type. If I can convert it to a 
    # number then I will ignore it.
    try:
        number = float(string)
        return number
    except:
        this_string_indexes = []
        words = string.split(" ")
       
        conversion_dictionary = {
                                  "column_name": column_name,
                                  "row_position": row_index,
                                  "index_list": index_list,
                                  "index_dictionary": index_dictionary,
                                  "word_indexes": word_indexes
        }  
        this_string_indexes = [convert_word_to_index(word, **conversion_dictionary) for word in words] 
        this_string_reference = {
                                 "source": "index",
                                 "indexes": this_string_indexes
        }
        #print(f"Converted string '{string}' to reference {this_string_reference}.")
        return this_string_reference


def convert_word_to_index(word, column_name, row_position, index_list, index_dictionary, word_indexes):
    #print(f"Converting word '{word}' to index.")
    if not isinstance(word, str):
        # I want to convert words to references and leave numbers as they are
        return ValueError(f"This word is not of type string: {word}.")
    
    #this_word_reference = word_references.get(word)
    this_word_locations = index_dictionary.get(word)
    if this_word_locations:
        # If the word already exists in the database then get the 
        # position of it in the primary index.
        word_index = word_indexes.get(word)
        if not word_index:
            return ValueError(f"Word '{word}' was not found in word_indexes: {word_indexes}.")
    else:
        # If the word does not yet exist in the database then
        # add a new word entry to the database
        word_locations_list = [{"source": column_name, "position": row_position}]
        #word_dictionary[word] = word_reference_list
        #word_references[word] = [{"source": "database/index.json", "index": row_index}]
        #word_references[word] = word_reference_list
        
        word_index = len(index_list)
        word_indexes[word] = word_index
        index_list.append({
                           "word": word,
                           "references": [{
                                           "source": column_name,
                                           "index": row_position
                                          }]
                          })
        index_dictionary[word] = word_locations_list
    #print(f"Converted word '{word}' to index {word_index}.")
    return word_index

def file_traversal_search(current_file_path, files_to_look_for, files_traversed=[]):
    """Find a path from the current file to one of the ones I am looking for.

    Args:
        current_file_path (str): The path of the current file.
        files_to_look_for (list): A list of eligible destination files.
        files_traversed (list): A list of the files that have already been traversed during search.

    Returns:
        files_traversed (list): Once a destination file has been found this function will return the list of files traversed.
    """ 

    # Add the current file to the list of files traversed
    files_traversed.append(current_file_path)
    print(current_file_path, files_to_look_for)    

    # Check if the current file is the one the function is looking for. If so, then
    # the function has completed its job and will return the list of files
    # that it traversed to find the file or files it was looking for.
    if current_file_path in files_to_look_for:
        return files_traversed

    with open(current_file_path, 'r') as file_handle:
        file_data = json.load(file_handle)
    # The path to the next file in the database is always stored as the last element.
    next_file_path = file_data[-1]
 
    if next_file_path in files_to_look_for:
        files_traversed.append(next_file_path)
        return files_traversed
    else:
        return file_traversal_search(next_file_path, files_to_look_for, files_traversed)

def find_query_loop(query_word_location_lists):
    # Add the first node to the end of the list to complete the loop
    query_word_location_lists.append(query_word_location_lists[0])

    edges = []
    for query_word_index, this_word_locations in enumerate(query_word_location_lists):
    
        # Break the loop once I reach the end of the list of words
        if query_word_index >= len(query_word_location_lists) - 1:
            break
        locations_to_look_for = query_word_location_lists[query_word_index + 1]
        files_to_look_for = [location["source"] for location in locations_to_look_for]
        for this_location in this_word_locations:

            # Find a path to the next location
            path = file_traversal_search(this_location["source"], files_to_look_for, files_traversed=[])
            next_source = path[-1]

            # Now that I have found a looping path between two adjacent
            # words in my query I want to calculate the minimum index
            # distance between those words in those source locations.
            this_source_locations = [location for location in this_word_locations if location["source"] == this_location["source"]]
            next_source_locations = [location for location in locations_to_look_for if location["source"] == next_source]

            this_location_indexes = set(location["index"] for location in this_source_locations)
            next_location_indexes = list(set(location["index"] for location in next_source_locations))

            if 0 in next_location_indexes:
                # Add every index of this word  as an index of the next

                next_location_indexes.remove(0)
 
            # First I need to find all of the locations that match
            # this source from my 
            index_pairs = list(itertools.product(this_location_indexes, next_location_indexes))
            index_products = [{"start": index_pair[0], "end": index_pair[1], "score": index_pair[0] * index_pair[1]} for index_pair in index_pairs]
        
            index_products = sorted(index_products, key=lambda index_product: index_product["score"])

            # I have deprecated this logic in favor of the above where I use a
            # list comprehension to remove any products with zero scores.
            optimal_index = index_products[0]
            if optimal_index["score"] == 0:
                optimal_index["score"] = 1
                # I need to change the variable index to an index of an actual
                # value. I do not know which word has an index of zero so I
                # will change both start and end indexes to the maximum.
                optimal_index["start"] = max([optimal_index["start"], optimal_index["end"]])
                optimal_index["end"] = max([optimal_index["start"], optimal_index["end"]])

            # Once I have found one of the files to look for I

            # current source to the source that I was looking for.
            path_dictionary = {

            }

    return edges

    # Always pick from the lowest scored edges
    if word_index >= len(word_edges):

    # Only edges that have the same start node as the previous end node
    # are eligible to be chosen. I can use a list comprehension to filter
    # out nodes that do not meet this criterion.
    if chosen_edges:
        previous_end = chosen_edges[-1]["end"]
        eligible_edges = [edge for edge in word_edges[word_index] if edge["start"] == previous_end]
    else:
        eligible_edges = word_edges[word_index]

    chosen_edge = eligible_edges[0]
    chosen_edges.append(chosen_edge)
    word_index += 1
    return choose_an_edge(word_edges, chosen_edges, word_index)

        discarded_edge = chosen_edges.pop(0)
